title: Couples and torque

learning_outcomes.text: understand that a couple is a pair of forces that acts to produce rotation only
define and apply the torque of a couple

external_knowledge: Force is a vector measured in newtons.
Clockwise and anticlockwise describe opposite turning directions.

prior_knowledge_summary: The weight of an object may be treated as acting at its centre of gravity.
The moment of one force about a point is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from that point to the force's line of action.
A single force can produce both a resultant force and a turning effect.
new_learning: Recognise a couple as two equal, opposite, parallel forces with separate lines of action.
Explain why a couple has zero resultant force but a non-zero turning effect.
Calculate torque using one force and the perpendicular separation of the two lines of action.
not_yet_taught: Using zero resultant force and zero resultant torque together as equilibrium conditions

blocks.heading: Why can a steering wheel turn without moving sideways?
content: Place one hand high on a steering wheel and the other low on it. Push with equal forces in opposite directions. The pushes cancel as a force, yet the wheel turns.
That seems contradictory only if we track force and ignore where each force acts. The separation between the two lines of action creates a pure turning effect.

figure.purpose: Open with the puzzle of zero resultant force but non-zero rotation.
figure.brief: Landscape 3:2 white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Show a steering wheel with one horizontal force to the right at its top and an equal horizontal force to the left at its bottom. Mark the separate parallel lines of action and a curved rotation arrow. Do not include a torque value or formula.
figure.alt_text: Equal opposite horizontal forces at the top and bottom of a steering wheel produce rotation.

blocks.heading: The four checks for a couple
content: A couple is a pair of forces that acts to produce rotation only. Check four features: the forces are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, parallel, and on separate lines of action.

Equal and opposite forces give zero resultant force. Separate lines of action make both forces turn the object in the same direction. If their lines of action were the same, there would be no separation and no couple torque.
A pair of unequal forces is not a couple. A pair that is equal and opposite but not parallel is not a couple either.

figure.purpose: Make the geometric conditions for a couple visually testable.
figure.brief: Landscape 3:2 white-paper colourful hand-drawn comparison. In a left panel show equal opposite parallel forces on separate lines with check marks. In a right panel show three rejected pairs: unequal, not parallel, and same line of action. Keep labels short and show no calculations.
figure.alt_text: A comparison distinguishes a true couple from unequal, non-parallel and same-line force pairs.

blocks.heading: Torque measures the strength of a couple
content: Definition to learn: the product of one of the forces and the perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the forces.
Calculation relationship to remember: torque equals one force multiplied by the perpendicular separation. Torque is measured in N m, force in N, and separation in m.

Use one force, not both forces added together. The separation already spans the two force lines. The lesson specification names a torque-formula ID that is absent from the controlled formula registry, so this lesson cites the exact controlled definition and does not invent a formula record.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: the product of one of the forces and the perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the forces

figure.purpose: Define the perpendicular separation used in torque without doubling the force.
figure.brief: Landscape 3:2 white-paper colourful hand-drawn force sketch. Draw two parallel force lines with equal opposite arrows labelled F, a right-angle separation bracket labelled s, and the words one force x perpendicular separation below. Highlight the word one beside one force only.
figure.alt_text: Two equal opposite force lines are separated perpendicularly, with torque found from one force and the separation.

blocks.heading: A wheel turned by two tangential forces
content: Two tangential forces of 16 N act in opposite directions at the left and right edges of a wheel. Their parallel lines of action are 0.30 m apart.
Use one force and the full perpendicular separation: torque = 16 x 0.30 = 4.8 N m. Both forces turn the wheel clockwise, so the torque is 4.8 N m clockwise.
Independent check using the centre: each force has a 0.15 m lever arm, so the two moments give 16 x 0.15 + 16 x 0.15 = 4.8 N m. This agrees with the couple formula.

figure.purpose: Connect the direct couple formula to two same-direction moments about the wheel centre.
figure.brief: Landscape 3:2 white-paper colourful hand-drawn worked layout. Show a wheel with two 16 N tangential forces, full line separation 0.30 m, half distances 0.15 m, clockwise arrows, the direct calculation 16 x 0.30, and the check 16 x 0.15 + 16 x 0.15. Keep both routes visually distinct.
figure.alt_text: A wheel example calculates 4.8 N m directly and checks it using two moments about the centre.

blocks.heading: A couple can move without changing its torque
content: Imagine lifting a tray by pushing up at one edge and down at the other with equal parallel forces. Sliding both force lines together across the tray changes their position, but not their magnitude or perpendicular separation.

The torque therefore stays the same because one force and the force-line separation contain no pivot position. This is different from the moment of one force, whose perpendicular distance is measured from a chosen point.
Increasing the force or increasing the perpendicular separation increases torque in direct proportion. Doubling either one doubles the turning effect.

figure.purpose: Contrast position-independent couple torque with a single-force moment about a point.
figure.brief: Landscape 3:2 white-paper colourful hand-drawn sequence. Show the same tray in two positions with an identical equal-opposite force pair shifted sideways while separation s stays fixed. Add a small separate sketch of one force whose distance is measured from point O. Do not introduce equilibrium equations.
figure.alt_text: A force pair shifts across a tray with unchanged separation while a single-force moment is measured from point O.

blocks.heading: Zero resultant force does not mean zero turning effect
content: It feels reasonable to say that equal and opposite forces cancel completely. They do cancel as a resultant force, so the object's centre does not receive a sideways push from the pair.
The idea fails when the force lines are separate. Each force turns the object in the same direction, so their turning effects add. A true couple produces rotation only, not zero effect.
Do not turn this into the full equilibrium rule yet. The next module will combine force and torque conditions carefully.

figure.purpose: Separate translational cancellation from rotational addition.
figure.brief: Landscape 3:2 white-paper colourful hand-drawn split panel. Left: equal opposite vector arrows add to zero resultant force. Right: the same separated arrows each have a clockwise curved arrow, and the curved effects add. Include no full equilibrium condition.
figure.alt_text: Equal opposite forces cancel translationally but their separated turning effects add.

blocks.heading: Choose the distance that belongs to the turning effect
content: For one force about a point, use the previous lesson route: force times perpendicular distance from the point to that force's line of action.
For a couple, first confirm equal, opposite, parallel forces on separate lines. Then use one force times the perpendicular separation between the two force lines.

Always state clockwise or anticlockwise when direction matters. A zero resultant force from a couple does not remove its torque. The next lesson may assume you can keep these two turning-effect routes distinct.

evidence_basis.p1_status: deferred by the controlled lesson specification
evidence_basis.evidence_scope_note: Whole official questions were reviewed. Only couple recognition, torque, perpendicular-distance and prior moment demands are used; the principle of moments, complete equilibrium, springs, upthrust and later energy methods are excluded from required learning.

concepts_taught: a couple is an equal, opposite, parallel force pair on separate lines of action
a couple has zero resultant force and a non-zero turning effect
couple torque depends on one force and perpendicular line separation
couple torque is independent of the chosen reference point
misconceptions_addressed: Equal and opposite forces always have no effect.
Torque of a couple uses twice the magnitude of one force.
Any two opposite forces form a couple.
The separation is measured along an object rather than perpendicularly between force lines.
next_lesson_can_assume: Recognition of a couple from its four force conditions.
Use of one force multiplied by perpendicular force-line separation for couple torque.
Distinction between a single-force moment about a point and torque of a couple.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Complete translational and rotational equilibrium conditions.
